entries.name: Adam
entries.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
entries.definition: Stochastic gradient optimization using bias-corrected exponential estimates of first and second gradient moments to scale parameter updates.
entries.mechanism: The update divides the bias-corrected first moment by the square root of the bias-corrected second raw moment plus a numerical stabilizer.
entries.identity_notes: Adam specifies adaptive moment-based updates; the local SGD concept does not require these estimates. It is an optimizer, not a training task or a trained model.

aio_mappings.rationale: An optimizer can implement parameter fitting, but the pinned TrainingStrategy definition uses a preprocessing genus; no subclass relationship is asserted.

limitations: No universal convergence or benchmark superiority claim is curated.
AdamW, AdaMax and other variants require their own identity assessment.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract proposes adaptive lower-order moment estimates for stochastic optimization and reports favorable experiments. Those performance and convergence statements are not adopted as universal properties.

entries.name: Proximal policy optimization
entries.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
entries.definition: A family of policy-gradient algorithms alternating collected interaction data with repeated optimization of a surrogate objective using clipping or an adaptive KL penalty.
entries.mechanism: The clipped variant takes the minimum of unclipped and clipped probability-ratio advantage terms; another variant uses an adaptive KL-divergence penalty, and the algorithm performs multiple minibatch epochs on collected trajectories.
entries.locator: Sections 3–5, equations 7–8 and Algorithm 1, PDF/printed pp. 3–5
entries.identity_notes: PPO is a policy-optimization algorithm family. It is distinct from the broad reinforcement-learning task and from DPO's direct preference-fitting objective; PPO is not synonymous with its clipped variant alone.

aio_mappings.rationale: PPO is a particular policy-gradient procedure within reinforcement-learning practice; the AIO class denotes the broader task.

limitations: Clipping the surrogate objective is not an explicit hard bound on all policy changes.
The record covers the original clipped and KL-penalized variants without asserting task-independent performance.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract introduces surrogate objectives that allow repeated minibatch updates after environment sampling. Reported robotics and Atari comparisons are experiments, not defining properties.

entries.name: Soft actor-critic
entries.title: Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor
entries.definition: An off-policy actor-critic algorithm fitting a stochastic policy and soft value functions under a reward-plus-policy-entropy objective.
entries.mechanism: Experience is retained in a replay buffer; value and policy networks are updated from sampled batches, with the policy objective balancing action value against log policy probability.
entries.locator: Section 3.2 equation 1 and section 4.2 equations 5–13 / Algorithm 1, PDF pp. 3–5
entries.identity_notes: SAC specifies an off-policy maximum-entropy actor-critic procedure. It is not a synonym for all reinforcement learning, for PPO, or for every entropy-regularized algorithm.

aio_mappings.rationale: SAC is a particular algorithm for policy learning, whereas the pinned AIO target is a broad machine-learning task.

limitations: The inspected 2018 method includes a state-value approximator; later variants are not automatically identical in implementation.
Tabular soft-policy-iteration theory does not by itself certify convergence of arbitrary neural function approximators.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract proposes off-policy actor-critic learning with an entropy-augmented objective and evaluates continuous control. Stability and benchmark advantages remain claims about those experiments.

entries.name: GraphSAGE
entries.title: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs
entries.definition: An inductive graph representation architecture that learns neighborhood aggregation functions to generate node embeddings from features.
entries.mechanism: At each depth, sampled neighbor representations are aggregated and combined with a node's current representation through learned transformations; parameters are shared across nodes.
entries.locator: Section 3.1, Algorithm 1 and Neighborhood definition, PDF/printed pp. 3–4
entries.identity_notes: GraphSAGE learns an embedding-generating function, unlike individually fitted transductive node embeddings. The broad AIO graph-convolutional category does not require the named sampling-and-aggregation framework.

aio_mappings.rationale: Learned aggregation and transformation layers form an artificial neural network; this target is broader than the specific graph architecture.
The pinned definition broadly describes learning on graph structure, but GraphSAGE has its own inductive sampling/aggregation construction; a narrower GCN algorithm is not equated with it.

limitations: The paper describes multiple aggregators; no single mean or pooling variant defines the entire framework.
Inductive construction does not guarantee accurate embeddings for every unseen graph or feature distribution.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract distinguishes an embedding-generating function from per-node transductive parameters and tests unseen nodes and graphs. Its benchmark results are not universal generalization guarantees.

entries.name: Graph attention network
entries.title: Graph Attention Networks
entries.definition: A graph neural architecture that updates node representations using learned attention weights over graph neighborhoods.
entries.mechanism: Shared transformations and a learned attention function produce neighborhood scores, softmax normalizes those scores, and their weighted feature combinations form updated node representations.
entries.identity_notes: The original GAT architecture is distinct from a generic attention layer and from graph-convolution methods that do not use its learned neighborhood attention. GATv2 and other revisions are outside this identity.

aio_mappings.rationale: Graph attentional layers are learned neural computations, so the general artificial-neural-network target is broader.
Both use graph structure, but the GAT paper defines a specific learned attention mechanism; the mapping does not equate named GAT and GCN algorithms.

limitations: The record uses the revised ICLR 2018 paper, including its specified attention nonlinearity.
Attention coefficients are computation weights; no general causal-explanation or benchmark-superiority claim is made.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract proposes masked self-attention over graph neighborhoods and reports transductive and inductive experiments. Its architectural contribution is learned neighbor weighting, not proof that weights explain causality.

entries.name: Graph isomorphism network
entries.title: How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?
entries.definition: A graph neural architecture using multilayer perceptrons on sums of neighboring representations and a separately weighted self-representation.
entries.mechanism: Each update applies an MLP to the sum of neighbor states and (1 + epsilon) times the current node state, with epsilon fixed or learned.
entries.locator: Section 4.1, Corollary 6 and equation 4.1, PDF/printed p. 5 of arXiv v3
entries.identity_notes: GIN is the named sum-and-MLP architecture, not the graph-isomorphism decision problem, all graph neural networks, or all architectures as expressive as a Weisfeiler–Lehman test.

aio_mappings.rationale: The architecture uses learned multilayer perceptrons to transform graph-node states; the AIO neural-network category is broader.
The AIO category describes graph-structured neural computation broadly; the GIN construction has a specific aggregation and self-weighting rule.

limitations: The equation is taken from revised v3; the earlier v1 expression lacks the separately parameterized self weighting.
No claim that GIN solves arbitrary graph isomorphism or that every trained finite network attains the theoretical expressivity bound is curated.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract analyzes neighborhood-aggregation expressivity and proposes an architecture connected to the Weisfeiler–Lehman test. The method is not an unrestricted graph-isomorphism solver.

entries.name: SHapley additive explanations
entries.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
entries.definition: An additive feature-attribution framework assigning Shapley values to a prediction through a specified function for evaluating feature subsets.
entries.mechanism: In the paper's conditional-expectation formulation, feature attributions average marginal changes in expected model output across feature orderings and combine with a baseline prediction.
entries.locator: Sections 3–4, equations 8–12 and Figure 1, PDF/printed pp. 4–5
entries.identity_notes: SHAP denotes the attribution framework, not the software package or any one estimator such as Kernel SHAP. LIME instead fits a locally weighted surrogate objective that need not recover these Shapley values.

aio_mappings.rationale: The shared theme is explaining predictions, but SHAP is a general attribution framework and the AIO target is a type of language model; neither equivalence nor subclasshood is asserted.

limitations: Feature-subset evaluation and dependence assumptions affect the interpretation; the paper distinguishes conditional expectations from independence approximations.
Attribution values do not by themselves establish causal effects or that a model is safe to deploy.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract unifies additive feature-attribution methods and introduces SHAP with proposed axioms and estimators. The framework should be distinguished from any single implementation or estimator.

entries.name: Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations
entries.title: Why Should I Trust You?: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
entries.definition: A prediction-explanation method fitting an interpretable surrogate to locally weighted samples of a model's behavior.
entries.mechanism: Perturbed interpretable inputs are mapped back to model inputs and labeled by model outputs; fitting balances a locality-weighted fidelity loss against surrogate complexity.
entries.identity_notes: LIME is a local surrogate explanation procedure, not an inherently explainable model, a guarantee of global fidelity, or the separate SP-LIME representative-selection method.

aio_mappings.rationale: Both concern explaining predictions, but LIME is a general post-hoc algorithm rather than a language-model class; the mapping makes no LLM-specific efficacy assertion.

limitations: The source explicitly distinguishes local fidelity from global fidelity.
Choice of interpretable representation, neighborhood and surrogate family is part of the method's scope; explanations are not a general certification of trustworthiness.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The abstract proposes local interpretable surrogates and separately introduces SP-LIME for representative explanations. User-study claims are distinct from the local fitting mechanism.

version_assessment: Used GIN v3 after comparing its epsilon-weighted update to the earlier v1 expression.
GAT v3 explicitly includes LeakyReLU; the v1 expression differs.
Used SAC v2 and GraphSAGE v4; earlier PDFs were inspected but are not the native-record authority.
